prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many atoms to be interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and trap-induced shifts, and for its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my preferred prize and I have tested it against the chair's questions rather than only restating it. What the lattice clock adds beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes can be said in one sentence. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and comb-based spectroscopy, which made optical frequencies countable, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions, whose clocks are limited by having one absorber. Katori's proposal of a magic-wavelength optical lattice, in which the light shift of the clock transition cancels so that the trap does not perturb the clock, makes it possible to interrogate thousands of neutral atoms at once without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is a new architecture and a new route to statistical power, and it is what took clocks to 10^-18 and into millimetre-scale redshift measurements. The test that the prize identifies a discovery or invention and the people responsible for it is met more cleanly here than anywhere else on the list: two names, one for the concept and its first realisation, one for carrying it to the extreme of performance, with independent reproduction at several national laboratories. I would write the citation so that it names the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly and does not mention the comb or ion clocks, so that it claims neither lineage. My preference is unchanged from round 1. I did consider moving to B004 after reading Johansson and Pearce, and I do not rule it out for the vote, but their arguments strengthen the merit of B004 without removing the credit gap, which still weighs on my judgement.
statement.case_against: The continuity objection is real and I do not think it can be fully dissolved: a colleague who sees the lattice clock as a very large improvement in precision within a lineage already honoured by two prizes will not be moved by my wording. The credit boundary toward Al+ and other ion-clock groups and toward other lattice-clock laboratories (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo) is a judgement, not a fact. The redefinition of the second has not yet occurred, so part of the impact is prospective. And B004 has the broadest opening support and the longest confirmation record; if the committee puts conceptual novelty above demonstrated measurement capability, it is a legitimate and stronger choice on that axis, with a real credit gap of its own (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang).

responses.point: Johansson prefers B004 on a narrow Z2 quantum spin Hall citation, argues that the physics is distinct from the 2016 prize, and lists B006 as a first alternative while asking whether there is a fairer way to treat B006 given the comb and ion-clock recognition.
responses.response: Your answer to the 2016 overlap is persuasive: symmetry-protected edge transport without a field is a distinct idea. I would apply the same test to B006, and I think it passes. The lattice clock is distinct from the comb and the single-ion clock for the same kind of reason, because it needs a new trapping concept and not just better lasers. Where I differ is the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang step. Tightening the citation to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect makes the claim narrower, but the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested still came from outside the credited names, and no wording repairs that. For B006 the corresponding boundary is a question of degree about other clock groups, not the absence of a decisive step. That asymmetry is why I am not yet moving.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B006 on concept plus demonstrated 10^-18 reproduction, and discloses a doctoral-period stay in John Hall's laboratory, asking whether this calls for recusal.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your case and I would anchor the citation exactly as you do, on the lattice concept. On your disclosure, my own view is that a past laboratory stay in the milieu from which Ye emerged, without collaboration, is a connection to record and not a reason to recuse, much as Lindroth reads it. I would, however, accept the committee asking both of us to say plainly that neither has a collaboration or supervisory tie with Katori or Ye. Your point that the comparison with B004 turns on novelty against reach is the right axis, and I would add that the clock's reach is demonstrated and not promised.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B006 first as the only mature, cleanly attributed candidate with a small well-defined group, and states she would not stand in the way of B004 if novelty is to dominate.
responses.response: I agree that no other candidate combines maturity, clean attribution and a small credited group. I would add one condition for the citation, which in round 1 you left implicit: it should say what is new. As an atomic physicist you may be better placed than I am to judge whether the ion-clock community would accept that the lattice is a different thing, but I believe the many-atom, magic-wavelength architecture is a clear answer and I would put it in the citation text. I also share your openness to B004, which is why it is my first alternative and not a candidate I resist.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B009, arguing that waiting for the pairing mechanism may mean waiting indefinitely, that the credited names cover theory plus experiment, and that B004 is the safer alternative on maturity.
responses.response: Your argument that a citation can be framed around flat bands and not the mechanism is fair, and I have moved B009 from a hesitant mention to a named alternative. I still disagree on timing, for a reason from my own experimental practice: the decisive experiments are seven to eight years old, strain and twist-angle disorder are still being separated from intrinsic behaviour, and the experimental credit rests on Jarillo-Herrero without Cao and others. If the mechanism question is truly orthogonal to the discovery, that will remain true in a few years, and the prize loses nothing by waiting. I do not think that is a reason to block B009 in the vote, but it is a reason not to place it first.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B043 to B004 on the grounds that Z2 theory plus HgTe observation is a sharp idea tested against nature, confirmed for fifteen to twenty years, with an interpretation that is stable.
responses.response: I share your respect for a prediction that can be falsified and was not, and I take seriously that you moved from your own first choice on the merits. On that criterion the lattice clock also qualifies: magic-wavelength cancellation was a definite prediction of an engineering and spectroscopic kind, tested and then pushed from 10^-16 to 10^-18 in several laboratories. The difference is that B004 has an unresolved credit gap, and you yourself record the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as a real reservation. I would rather award the candidate whose credit we can defend in a citation.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B002 to B004, values a falsifiable prediction confirmed in the laboratory, and wants the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap stated openly in the record; he also suggests that B006 might overtake B004 once the redefinition of the second is closer.
responses.response: I agree that the gap should be stated openly in the record for whichever configuration goes forward, and I would extend that to the continuity objection against B006. On your point about the redefinition of the second, I would not make it a reason to wait. The prize is for the invention and its demonstrated performance, which stand today, and a redefinition would be a consequence of the work and not a condition of it. Waiting on an administrative decision would let timing, not science, set the award.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct new concept or as an incremental step within the lineage of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this is the decisive judgement for B006 and the supplied text does not settle it.

Whether ion-clock groups or other lattice-clock laboratories have a claim that makes the Katori and Ye credit look incomplete, and where exactly Ye's contribution sits relative to the comb lineage, which Johansson raised.

Whether the committee accepts a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp citation without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I would not oppose it if the boundary is stated openly, and I may use B004 as my second choice in the vote.
I cannot assess the aberration-corrected electron optics case (B012) independently of my own field, and I have set it aside for the vote.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. First, my own field is electron microscopy, so I cannot claim independence on B012 (Rose, Haider, Krivanek); I no longer prefer it and treat it as outside my configuration. Second, my profile records a University of Tokyo fellowship, a JSPS fellowship and long exchanges with Japanese universities, and Katori is at the University of Tokyo. I know of no collaboration, supervisory or personal tie with Katori or Ye, and I regard this as an institutional connection to record and not a ground for recusal, but I leave that to the committee, and I note that Kroll's disclosure is of a similar kind. Göran Johansson is a colleague at Chalmers, which bears on our relations and not on any shortlisted candidate. I have no documented connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero.
